steps.text: Part 2 of 4: Double check: how to see it, set it up and stop it. This part covers Why it works, and when it fails. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.prompt: A piece gives double check and stands next to the king. When can the king take it?

fields.label: The king can take it:
options: whenever it is a minor piece
only if no white piece attacks that square, the other checker included
never: only moves away are legal
only if the other checker is a knight
fields.answer: only if no white piece attacks that square, the other checker included

steps.caption: White to move, in double check: the knight on f5 and the rook on c3 both attack the king. Which White pieces can help?
steps.chapter: Why it works, and when it fails

line.say: Only the king can move. Capturing or blocking one checker would leave the other check standing.
Black's knight takes the rook on g7.

claims.statement: White is in check.
Two black pieces attack the king.
Every legal move is a king move.

steps.text: **Why only the king can answer.** A single check can be met three ways: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. A capture or a block deals with one checker, and the other check is still there. So the king must move. That includes the king *capturing* a checker, if the checker stands next to the king and nothing protects it.

steps.title: The uncovered line must be open
steps.prompt: In the second position a black pawn stands on e6. In the third, the black a-pawn has moved one square.

steps.caption: A bare board. White to move. The bishop on e5 blocks the rook's file.

line.say: The bishop leaves the file and checks from d6: two checks, and the bishop is next to the king.
Nothing protects the bishop, so the king simply takes it.

claims.statement: The bishop move is legal.
After the bishop moves, two white pieces attack the king.
No white piece protects the bishop on d6.

steps.caption: The same board with one change: a white pawn stands on c5.

line.say: The bishop gives the same double check.
The pawn on c5 protects the bishop, so the king cannot take it. It has to run.

claims.statement: The bishop move is legal.
After the bishop moves, two white pieces attack the king.
The pawn on c5 protects the bishop on d6.

steps.text: **What a double check needs, and what makes it win.** It needs an open line once the front piece leaves, and a front piece that checks from its new square. Miss either and you have one check, which can be blocked or captured. It wins when the king cannot take the checker and every flight square is covered. Even then the forced king move buys a free move, because the king had to answer. That free move can bring mate, a fork or an undefended piece.

steps.text: **Which piece moves in front? [V] our data.** In 39 Lichess puzzles (CC0, chosen for the double-check theme, so not a fair sample of games) whose key move is a true double check, the front piece was a knight 25 times, a pawn 8, a rook 4, a bishop 2, and never a queen or king in this sample. A knight always checks from two squares away, so the king can never take it (geometry). [H] That may explain why knights lead the count.

**Remember.** A double check is two checks at once, so only the king can answer. It needs an open line behind the front piece, and that piece must check from where it lands. Ask: can the king take a checker, or step to a safe square? If so, it fails.
